pos: n. (the felonious taking and carrying away of another's goods)
etymology: Latin latrocinium, robbery. Webster: theft; the act of taking and carrying away the goods or property of another feloniously. Simple larceny is theft without an aggravating circumstance. Mixed larceny adds the taking from a house or person, as in burglary or robbery.
biblical_def:
Thou shalt not steal. Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth. Ye shall not steal, neither deal falsely, neither lie one to another. The flying roll in Zechariah carries a curse, and every one that stealeth shall be cut off on this side according to it.

Larceny is theft named by the court. Scripture does not wait for the value of twelve pence. The taking and carrying away of a neighbour's goods is the eighth commandment whether the statute calls it petty or grand. The cure Paul names is not a finer distinction. It is labor, and a hand that gives.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): theft; the act of taking and carrying away the goods or property of another feloniously. Simple larceny is theft without an atrocious circumstance. Mixed larceny includes taking from a house or person.
webster_full: LARCENY, n. Theft; the act of taking and carrying away the goods or property of another feloniously.
Simple larceny is theft not accompanied with any atrocious circumstance.
Mixed or compound larceny includes the aggravation of taking from one's house or person, as in burglary or robbery.
scriptures: Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth.
Ye shall not steal, neither deal falsely, neither lie one to another.

Then said he unto me, This is the curse that goeth forth over the face of the whole earth: for every one that stealeth shall be cut off as on this side according to it; and every one that sweareth shall be cut off as on that side according to it.
corruption_summary: The age treats a small taking as not really theft, as if the eighth commandment began at a price the court invented.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster's petty and grand are statute lines. They are not moral lines. Zechariah's curse does not ask the value of the thing stolen.

The other corruption is the refusal of Ephesians 4:28. A man who has stolen is not finished when he stops. He is told to labor, and to give. Larceny's opposite is not a clean record. It is a working hand.
roots_summary: Latin latrocinium. The biblical charge is theft (Exo 20:15) and the thief who must steal no more (Eph 4:28).
roots_lines: Taking and carrying away is the legal picture. The commandment does not require the carrying to be far.
Zechariah 5:3 puts the stealer and the false swearer on the two sides of one curse.
usage: Thou shalt not steal — the commandment under every grade of larceny.
Let him that stole steal no more — the apostolic end of the habit.

pos: n. (nocturnal house-breaking with intent to commit a felony)
etymology: From burgh, a dwelling, and an old word for theft. Webster: the crime of nocturnal house-breaking, with intent to commit a felony. There must be a breaking and an entry, and the act must be in the night.
biblical_def:
If a thief be found breaking up, and be smitten that he die, there shall no blood be shed for him. In the dark they dig through houses, which they had marked for themselves in the daytime. Joel's locust-army enters in at the windows like a thief.

Burglary is theft that breaks the house. Scripture does not use the statute word, but it knows the man found breaking up, and the men who dig through houses in the dark. The house is the neighbour's shelter. To break it at night is not a bolder form of borrowing. It is an attack on the place God gave a man to lie down.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the crime of nocturnal house-breaking, with an intent to commit a felony. There must be an actual breaking and an entry, done in the night, in a mansion house or a building that is part of it.
webster_full: BURGLARY, n. The act or crime of nocturnal house breaking, with an intent to commit a felony.
The act must be committed in the night. There must be an actual breaking and an entry.
The act must also be done with an intent to commit felony.
scriptures: If a thief be found breaking up, and be smitten that he die, there shall no blood be shed for him.
In the dark they dig through houses, which they had marked for themselves in the daytime: they know not the light.
They shall run to and fro in the city; they shall run upon the wall, they shall climb up upon the houses; they shall enter in at the windows like a thief.
corruption_summary: The age treats a broken house as a property claim, and forgets that the night entry is an attack on a man's shelter.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 22:2 does not romanticize the killing. It names the thief found breaking up, and it refuses to call the householder a murderer for striking him in that act. The breaking is the crime.
Job 24:16 adds the marking by day and the digging by night. Burglary is planned. The men know not the light. That is the moral picture under the statute.
roots_summary: No single biblical headword. The field is the thief found breaking up (Exo 22:2) and those who dig through houses in the dark (Job 24:16).
roots_lines: Breaking and entering is Webster's pair. Scripture's breaking up is the same pair in older English.
Joel 2:9 uses the thief at the window as a picture of invasion. The house is not safe because the door was latched.
usage: If a thief be found breaking up — the law's name for the night entry.
In the dark they dig through houses — burglary as a way of life.

pos: n. (the malicious burning of another man's dwelling)
etymology: From Latin ardere, to burn. Webster: in law, the malicious burning of a dwelling house or outhouse of another man, which by the common law is felony.
biblical_def:
If fire break out, and catch in thorns, so that the stacks of corn, or the standing corn, or the field, be consumed therewith; he that kindled the fire shall surely make restitution. Samson set brands on fire and let them go into the standing corn of the Philistines, and burnt up both the shocks and the standing corn, with the vineyards and olives.

Arson is a fire kindled against another man's house or field. Scripture requires restitution when a fire a man kindled consumes his neighbour's corn. Samson's brands were an act of war, recorded as such, not as a permitted private burning. Malice is the difference between an escaped spark and a set fire.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the malicious burning of a dwelling house or outhouse of another man, which by the common law is felony.
webster_full: ARSON, n. In law, the malicious burning of a dwelling house or outhouse of another man, which by the common law is felony.
The definition of this crime is varied by statutes. The common-law core is a malicious burning of another man's dwelling.
scriptures: If fire break out, and catch in thorns, so that the stacks of corn, or the standing corn, or the field, be consumed therewith; he that kindled the fire shall surely make restitution.
And when he had set the brands on fire, he let them go into the standing corn of the Philistines, and burnt up both the shocks, and also the standing corn, with the vineyards and olives.
corruption_summary: The age treats a set fire as a statement, so that malicious burning is praised when the burner dislikes the owner.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 22:6 does not ask whether the kindler had a cause. He that kindled the fire shall surely make restitution. The neighbour's corn is not a symbol. It is food.

Webster's malicious is the moral word the slogan drops. A fire that escapes is a debt. A fire that is set against a dwelling is a felony. Scripture already requires the debt. The statute names the felony.
roots_summary: Latin ardere, to burn. The biblical field is the kindled fire that consumes a neighbour's field (Exo 22:6).
roots_lines: Restitution is the first biblical answer. The field is consumed. The kindler pays.
Judges 15:5 is recorded as Samson's war, not as a model for private men with a grievance.
usage: He that kindled the fire shall surely make restitution — the law under every set blaze.
He let them go into the standing corn — a fire sent, not a spark that escaped.

pos: n. (reveling; indulgence in excessive feasting; also the public tumult that belongs with it)
etymology: From riot. Webster's noun is brief: a reveling. The participle is reveling; indulging in excessive feasting. Scripture uses the same family for the night feast and for the disorder that walks with it.
biblical_def:
Let us walk honestly, as in the day; not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying. They that count it pleasure to riot in the day time are spots and blemishes. Paul has already listed revellings among the works that shut a man out of the kingdom.

Rioting is the feast that will not stay in its house. It is noisy, excessive, and public. Romans 13:13 sets it beside drunkenness and wantonness, and commands the saint to walk as in the day. A church that joins the riot and calls it fellowship has left that sentence.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a reveling. The participle is reveling; indulging in excessive feasting.
webster_full: RIOTING, participle. Reveling; indulging in excessive feasting.
scriptures: Let us walk honestly, as in the day; not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying.

And shall receive the reward of unrighteousness, as they that count it pleasure to riot in the day time. Spots they are and blemishes, sporting themselves with their own deceivings while they feast with you;
Envyings, murders, drunkenness, revellings, and such like: of the which I tell you before, as I have also told you in time past, that they which do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God.
corruption_summary: The age calls rioting a protest or a party, so that the night feast Paul forbids is baptized as a cause or a celebration.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 13:13 does not leave rioting in the category of high spirits. It stands with drunkenness, chambering, and strife. The walk of the day excludes it.
Peter's riot in the day time is worse, not better. The men who count it pleasure are spots at the feast of the church. A public tumult that begins in that pleasure is not thereby made righteous.
roots_summary: Greek komos (G2970) stands behind reveling; kōmos and the riot of 2 Peter 2:13 share the same family of excess. Romans 13:13 uses rioting for the night disorder.
roots_lines: Webster's reveling is the old sense. Paul's list keeps it with drunkenness.
Second Peter 2:13 moves the riot into the daylight and into the church's feast. That is the aggravation.
usage: Not in rioting and drunkenness — the apostolic walk.
They that count it pleasure to riot in the day time — spots at the table.

etymology: From brawl, to quarrel noisily. Webster's noun is one line: the act of quarreling.
biblical_def:
It is better to dwell in a corner of the housetop, than with a brawling woman in a wide house. The proverb repeats the sentence. A bishop must be no striker, not a brawler. The wide house does not cure the quarrel. The corner of the roof is better than the room where the strife never stops.

Brawling is quarrel as a habit. It is not one hard word in a true dispute. It is the noise that makes a house unlivable and a church unfit for an officer. Scripture would rather a man have a small quiet place than a large house ruled by the quarrel.
webster_full: BRAWLING, n. The act of quarreling.
scriptures: It is better to dwell in a corner of the housetop, than with a brawling woman in a wide house.
It is better to dwell in the corner of the housetop, than with a brawling woman and in a wide house.
Not given to wine, no striker, not greedy of filthy lucre; but patient, not a brawler, not covetous;
corruption_summary: The age calls brawling passion, so that a house or a church that cannot stop quarreling is praised for being real.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs does not treat the brawling as a communication style. It treats it as a reason to prefer the roof. The wide house is not worth the noise.
First Timothy 3:3 bars the brawler from the office. Patience is the opposite virtue named in the same verse. A man who must have the last loud word is not ready to oversee the church.
roots_summary: The Hebrew picture in Proverbs 21:9 is the contentious, brawling house. Greek amachos (G269) in 1 Timothy 3:3 is not a brawler, not a fighter.
roots_lines: The housetop is the proverb's measure. Quiet in a small place outranks space with strife.
The officer must be patient, not a brawler. The qualification is negative because the habit disqualifies.
usage: Better to dwell in a corner of the housetop — the proverb's judgment on brawling.
Not a brawler — the bar on the church officer.

pos: n. (the unlawful killing of a man without malice aforethought)
etymology: English, man and slaughter. Webster's general sense is the killing of a man. His legal sense is the unlawful killing of a man without malice, express or implied. It may be voluntary, upon a sudden heat, or involuntary, in the commission of an unlawful act. It differs from murder because murder requires malice prepense.
biblical_def:
If a man lie not in wait, but God deliver him into his hand; then I will appoint thee a place whither he shall flee. If he thrust him suddenly without enmity, or have cast upon him any thing without laying of wait, the cities of refuge receive the slayer who killeth any person at unawares.

Manslaughter, in the legal sense, is a killing without the lying in wait that makes murder. Scripture does not call that killing nothing. It appoints a city of refuge. The slayer flees. He does not go home as if no man had died. The distinction from murder is the absence of enmity and of laying in wait. The blood is still blood.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): in law, the unlawful killing of a man without malice, express or implied. It differs from murder in not proceeding from malice prepense. It differs from excusable homicide, being done in consequence of some unlawful act.
webster_full: MANSLAUGHTER, n. In a general sense, the killing of a man.
In law, the unlawful killing of a man without malice, express or implied. This may be voluntary, upon a sudden heat, or involuntary, in the commission of some unlawful act.
Manslaughter differs from murder in not proceeding from malice prepense or deliberate, which is essential to constitute murder.
scriptures: And if a man lie not in wait, but God deliver him into his hand; then I will appoint thee a place whither he shall flee.
But if he thrust him suddenly without enmity, or have cast upon him any thing without laying of wait,
Then ye shall appoint you cities to be cities of refuge for you; that the slayer may flee thither, which killeth any person at unawares.
corruption_summary: The age either collapses every killing into murder, or treats a killing without malice as if no one had died.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 21:13 keeps the distinction Scripture itself draws. Lying in wait is one case. God delivering a man into another's hand is another. The second still requires a place to flee. It is not a shrug.

Numbers 35:22 names the sudden thrust without enmity. That is the field of manslaughter. The city of refuge exists because the blood still cries, and because the avenger is not free to ignore the distinction.
roots_summary: No statute-word manslaughter. The biblical distinction is killing without lying in wait (Exo 21:13) and without enmity (Num 35:22), answered by the city of refuge.
roots_lines: Malice prepense is Webster's line between this word and murder. Scripture's line is laying of wait and enmity.
The slayer flees. That flight is the confession that a man is dead.
usage: If a man lie not in wait — the case that is not murder, and is not nothing.
The slayer may flee thither — the city, not a cleared name.

pos: n. (the security, or the surety, by which a prisoner is released to appear in court)
etymology: From an old word meaning to deliver. Webster: the person who procures the release of a prisoner by becoming surety for his appearance; also the security given. To bail is to liberate from arrest upon security that the person shall appear and answer.
biblical_def:
He that is surety for a stranger shall smart for it: and he that hateth suretiship is sure. My son, if thou be surety for thy friend, if thou hast stricken thy hand with a stranger, the warning has begun. At Thessalonica they took security of Jason, and of the other, and let them go.

Bail is suretyship in a court. A man binds himself that another will appear. Scripture does not forbid every security. Acts 17:9 records security taken so that Jason might be let go. It does warn the son that striking hands for another man's debt or appearance can cost him. The surety who hates the habit is called sure. The surety for a stranger shall smart.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the person or persons who procure the release of a prisoner by becoming surety for his appearance in court; also the security given for that release.
webster_full: BAIL, n. The person or persons who procure the release of a prisoner from custody, by becoming surety for his appearance in court.
The security given for the release of a prisoner from custody.
To bail is to set free from arrest upon security given that the person bailed shall appear and answer in court.
scriptures: He that is surety for a stranger shall smart for it: and he that hateth suretiship is sure.
My son, if thou be surety for thy friend, if thou hast stricken thy hand with a stranger,
And when they had taken security of Jason, and of the other, they let them go.
corruption_summary: The age treats bail as a formality, and forgets that the surety has bound his own goods to another man's appearance.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 11:15 is not against every pledge. It is against the light striking of hands. The man who is surety for a stranger shall smart. Bail is that smart waiting to happen if the prisoner does not appear.

Acts 17:9 shows security used to loose men who were not fleeing justice but were caught in a city's anger. The security was real. Jason's goods stood for their appearance. That is bail at its most sober.
roots_summary: The biblical field is suretyship (Pro 11:15; Pro 6:1) and security taken so that men might be let go (Act 17:9).
roots_lines: Webster's bail is a surety with a court date. Proverbs already knew the surety.
Hating suretiship is called sure. The habit of binding oneself for strangers is not wisdom.
usage: He that is surety for a stranger shall smart for it — the proverb under every bail bond.
They had taken security of Jason — bail that loosed the brethren and bound the host.

pos: n. (the crime of procuring a person to swear falsely, or to do a criminal act)
etymology: Latin subornare, to furnish or equip secretly, later to procure for a bad purpose. Webster: in law, the crime of procuring a person to take such a false oath as constitutes perjury. Also the crime of procuring one to do a criminal or bad action.
biblical_def:
Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour. A false witness shall not be unpunished. Then they suborned men, which said, We have heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses, and against God. Jezebel set two sons of Belial to bear witness against Naboth, saying, Thou didst blaspheme God and the king.

Subornation is the hiring or persuading of the false witness. The man who swears the lie is guilty. The man who procured him is guilty before the oath is taken. Acts 6:11 uses the verb. The witnesses against Stephen were not spontaneous. They were suborned. Naboth's vineyard was bought with the same crime.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the crime of procuring a person to take such a false oath as constitutes perjury. Also the crime of procuring one to do a criminal or bad action.
webster_full: SUBORNATION, n. In law, the crime of procuring a person to take such a false oath as constitutes perjury.
The crime of procuring one to do a criminal or bad action.
scriptures: Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour.
A false witness shall not be unpunished, and he that speaketh lies shall not escape.
Then they suborned men, which said, We have heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses, and against God.
And set two men, sons of Belial, before him, to bear witness against him, saying, Thou didst blaspheme God and the king. And then carry him out, and stone him, that he may die.
corruption_summary: The age prosecutes the false witness and often leaves the man who procured him in the chair.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 6:11 puts the guilt on they suborned. The sentence does not begin with the hired mouths. It begins with the procurers.

First Kings 21 is the exhibit. Jezebel did not need to swear. She set two sons of Belial to swear. Naboth died of subornation. A court that punishes only the mouth has not reached the crime Webster named.
roots_summary: Greek hypoballo (G5260) in Acts 6:11, to throw under, to instigate, to suborn. The moral charge is false witness (Exo 20:16).
roots_lines: The Greek is a throwing-under. The witness is put in place. He does not arrive on his own.
Proverbs 19:5 reaches the speaker of lies. Subornation reaches the one who put the lie in his mouth.
usage: They suborned men — the verb Acts uses for a procured witness.
Set two men, sons of Belial, before him — Jezebel's subornation of Naboth's death.
